title: Across the Curriculum: anti-, post-, semi-, super-, trans-
objectives: I can use the prefixes anti-, post-, semi-, super-, and trans- to work out the meaning of a word.
I can explain what ten prefix words mean in science, math, history, and sports.
I can find a base word inside a longer word and say what the prefix adds.
I can write about a school day using words from this unit.
rationale: Prefixes are the most efficient morphology a fifth grader can learn, because a handful of them unlock hundreds of words across subjects. This unit teaches five Latin and Greek prefixes that appear in math (semicircle), social studies (postwar), science (antifreeze, supersonic, transplant), sports (semifinal, postseason), and daily life (supervise, transfer, antisocial). Each word has a clear prefix and a recognizable base, so students can predict meaning by breaking the word apart: anti- means against, post- means after, semi- means half, super- means above or beyond, and trans- means across. The passage is a day of prefix hunting across the school day so that students see the same prefixes in different subjects. Telescope, microphone, aquatic, and thermal return so students can compare combining forms with true prefixes.

words.def: Unfriendly, or not wanting to spend time with other people.
words.ex: After a long day, Jamal felt antisocial and went for a quiet walk alone.
words.ex2: The antisocial cat hid under the porch whenever guests arrived.
words.nonExample: A friendly neighbor who chats with everyone is not antisocial.

apps.academic: Writers may describe a character as antisocial to show that he avoids other people.
apps.spoken: Don't mind me; I'm feeling a bit antisocial today.
apps.writing: Use antisocial with care: it can describe a mood or a harmful way of acting, so be sure of the sense.

cloze.s: The ___ new student ate lunch alone each day, and he turned down every invitation to join a table.

cloze2.s: After a noisy party, Rosa felt ___ and wanted nothing more than silence and a book.

misuse.s: The antisocial girl loved big parties and spent every minute talking to everyone.
misuse.why: Antisocial means unfriendly or not wanting company; loving parties is the opposite.

visual.alt: A person reading alone with a book.

words.def: A liquid that keeps water in a car engine from freezing.
words.ex: Dad added antifreeze to the car before the first snowfall.
words.ex2: Without antifreeze, the water in the engine could turn to ice on a bitter night.
words.nonExample: Plain water is not antifreeze, because it can still freeze.

apps.academic: Antifreeze works in a car's cooling system so the liquid does not freeze in cold weather.
apps.spoken: We need more antifreeze for the truck.
apps.writing: Use antifreeze for a liquid made to keep an engine from freezing.

cloze.s: Before winter, the mechanic filled the radiator with ___ so the engine would not freeze on icy mornings.

cloze2.s: The garage sold a green liquid called ___, which protects car engines in below-zero weather.

misuse.s: The antifreeze made the car's water turn to ice faster.
misuse.why: Antifreeze keeps liquid from freezing; it does not help it freeze.

words.def: The games played after the regular sports season ends.
words.ex: The team's hard work paid off when it reached the postseason for the first time.
words.ex2: Fans cheered for every postseason game, since a loss meant the end of the year.
words.nonExample: A practice game before the season begins is not a postseason game.

apps.academic: The postseason decides which team wins the championship.
apps.spoken: Our soccer team made the postseason!
apps.writing: Use postseason for the games that follow the regular season, such as the playoffs.

cloze.s: After winning most of its games, the team earned a place in the ___, where one loss would end its year.

cloze2.s: Fans bought tickets early for the ___, hoping their team would win the final trophy.

misuse.s: The postseason is the first game that happens before the regular season starts.
misuse.why: Postseason means after the regular season, not before.

visual.alt: A trophy beside a soccer ball.

words.frame: In the postseason, a team must ___.

words.def: Happening or existing in the years after a war.
words.ex: During the postwar years, many families moved to new houses outside the city.
words.ex2: The museum has photos of postwar markets that were busy with shoppers.
words.nonExample: A battle in the middle of a war is not a postwar event.

segs.m: armed fighting between groups or nations

apps.academic: Historians study postwar changes in housing, jobs, and schools.
apps.spoken: My grandmother grew up in the postwar years.
apps.writing: Use postwar for a time or event after a war has ended.

cloze.s: In the ___ years, soldiers returned home and began looking for work.

cloze2.s: The ___ city rebuilt its bridges, schools, and shops one block at a time.

misuse.s: The postwar battle took place while the fighting raged in the middle of the war.
misuse.why: Postwar means after a war; a battle in the middle of a war is not postwar.

visual.alt: A white dove flying over new houses.

words.ex: The teacher drew a semicircle on the board to show half of the pie.
words.ex2: The students sat in a semicircle around the storyteller.
words.nonExample: A full round ring is not a semicircle.

apps.academic: In geometry, a semicircle has a flat edge and a curved edge.
apps.writing: Use semicircle for a shape or an arrangement that is half of a circle.

cloze.s: The bridge's arch formed a perfect ___ over the stream.

cloze2.s: The chairs were arranged in a ___ facing the stage, with an open side at the back.

misuse.s: A semicircle is a full round circle with no flat edge.
misuse.why: A semicircle is half a circle, not a full one.

visual.alt: A half-circle rainbow beside a drawing tool.

words.def: A game or round that comes just before the final.
words.ex: Our school won the semifinal and will play for the championship on Friday.
words.ex2: In the semifinal, four teams fought for two places in the final.
words.nonExample: The championship game is not a semifinal.

apps.academic: In a tournament, the semifinal chooses the teams that play for the title.
apps.writing: Use semifinal for the round just before the last game.

cloze.s: Only the two winners of the ___ played in the championship the next day.

cloze2.s: The chess club lost in the ___ and missed the chance to play for the trophy.

misuse.s: The semifinal is the very last game, played after the championship.
misuse.why: A semifinal comes before the final, not after it.

visual.alt: A medal beside a silver second place.

words.frame: A team in the semifinal hopes to ___.

words.def: Faster than the speed of sound.
words.ex: A supersonic jet can cross the ocean in far less time than an ordinary plane.
words.ex2: When the plane went supersonic, people on the ground heard a loud boom.

apps.academic: Engineers design supersonic planes to fly faster than sound travels through air.
apps.writing: Use supersonic for speeds faster than the speed of sound.

cloze.s: The pilot flew the jet at ___ speed, faster than sound travels through air.

cloze2.s: A ___ aircraft makes a sudden loud boom as it passes the speed of sound.

misuse.s: The slow train was supersonic because it crept along at ten miles an hour.
misuse.why: Supersonic means faster than the speed of sound; ten miles an hour is slow.

words.def: To watch over and direct people or work to keep it safe.
words.ex: Two teachers supervise the playground during lunch.
words.ex2: A lifeguard must supervise the pool whenever children are swimming.
words.nonExample: Leaving young children alone at the pool is not to supervise them.

morph.note: The root vis takes a final e in this word: vis -> vise.

apps.academic: A scientist may supervise student helpers in the lab.
apps.spoken: Mom will supervise the bake sale.
apps.writing: Use supervise for watching over people or work to make sure it is done safely and well.

cloze.s: An adult must ___ the science experiment so that no student touches the hot plate.

cloze2.s: The coach will ___ practice, watching each player to make sure everyone stays safe.

misuse.s: The teacher agreed to supervise by leaving the room and not watching the class.
misuse.why: To supervise is to watch over; leaving and not watching is the opposite.

words.def: To dig up a plant and replant it somewhere else.

senses.def: To move an organ or tissue from one body to another in surgery.
senses.example: Doctors transplant a healthy kidney to help a patient whose kidneys have failed.

words.ex: In May, we will transplant the tomato seedlings from small pots into the garden.
words.ex2: The gardener carefully chose to transplant the rose bush into a sunnier spot.
words.nonExample: Watering a plant in the same pot is not to transplant it.
words.rel: moving a plant to a new place

apps.academic: Gardeners transplant seedlings once they are strong enough to grow outdoors.
apps.spoken: I helped Grandma transplant the herbs.
apps.writing: Use transplant for moving a living plant, or in medicine for moving an organ.

cloze.s: When the seedlings had grown tall, Ana helped ___ them from cups into the big garden bed.

cloze2.s: The roses were crowded, so the gardener decided to ___ half of them to the sunny side of the yard.

misuse.s: To transplant the bush, she left it in the same hole and never moved it.
misuse.why: To transplant is to move a plant to a new place, not leave it where it is.

words.def: To move from one place, school, or group to another.
words.ex: My cousin will transfer to our school next month.
words.ex2: Please transfer the soup from the pot to the bowls before it gets cold.
words.nonExample: Staying in the same seat all day is not to transfer.

apps.academic: Students may transfer to a new school when their families move.
apps.spoken: I'll transfer the files to your drive.
apps.writing: Use transfer for moving a person, an object, or information from one place to another.

cloze.s: After her family moved to Texas, Leila had to ___ to a new school halfway through the year.

cloze2.s: Please ___ the files from the old computer to the new one before you turn it off.

misuse.s: When I transfer to a new school, I stay in my old classroom forever.
misuse.why: To transfer is to move to a new place; staying in the old classroom is not a transfer.

passage.title: A Day of Prefix Hunting
paras: Ms. Chen challenged her class to hunt for prefixes all day. Before the bell, Mia watched her uncle fill his truck with antifreeze. "It keeps the engine from freezing on cold mornings," he said. Mia wrote anti- in her notebook and added its meaning, against.

In history, the class studied the postwar years, the time after a war ended, when many families built new homes. In math, Mia drew a semicircle on the board, half of a circle. At recess, a teacher came out to supervise the games, and Dev, who felt a little antisocial after a long week, read alone under the oak. Nobody minded.

After lunch, a new student arrived. She would transfer from another city and join their class. In science, Ms. Chen showed the class how to transplant bean seedlings from small cups into the garden bed. They also read about a supersonic jet, a plane that flies faster than the speed of sound.

That afternoon, the school soccer team won its semifinal, the game before the championship. The postseason, Ms. Chen explained, is the set of games after the regular season ends. By the end of the day, Mia's list held ten words and five prefixes: anti-, post-, semi-, super-, and trans-.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, what does the prefix anti- tell you about the word antifreeze?
qs.why: Mia writes that anti- means against, so antifreeze works against freezing.

choices: to move from one place or group to another
qs.why: The new student would transfer from another city and join the class, which means she would move from one school to another.

qs.q: How is a semifinal related to a championship?
choices: It is a smaller game in the middle of the season.
It is played by a different team.
It comes just before the championship.
qs.why: Ms. Chen says the semifinal is the game before the championship, so it comes right before the final.

qs.q: Why does the author say that Dev felt a little antisocial?
choices: He wanted to be alone and quiet for a while.
He was angry at the teacher.
He wanted to start a fight.
He did not know the rules of the game.
qs.why: Dev read alone under the oak after a long week, and nobody minded, so antisocial here means not in the mood for company.

qs.q: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Prefixes help us work out the meaning of many words across school subjects.
Soccer is the best game at school.
Seedlings need to be moved to the garden.
qs.why: Mia finds the same prefixes in math, history, science, and sports, so the passage shows how prefixes help with many words.

write.prompt: Write about a day at school or at home when you saw prefix words in different places. Use at least three words from this unit and underline each prefix.
write.frame: In ___, I saw the word ___. The prefix ___ means ___, so the word means ___.

study.task: Choose one prefix. Write three words that use it, break each word into its prefix and base, and say what the word means. Then predict what a new word with that prefix might mean and test your prediction in a sentence.

Write a sentence about something that happens in the postseason or in the postwar years.
Write a sentence that uses supervise and tells who is being watched.
Write a sentence that uses transplant or transfer and tells what is moved.

given: The gardener lifted the seedling carefully.
She planted it in a larger pot.
combine.model: After the gardener chose to transplant the seedling into a larger pot, it grew taller.

discuss: Which of the five prefixes do you think will help you most next year, and why?
What word do you know that uses anti-, post-, semi-, super-, or trans- that is not in this unit?
How can a shy person be different from an antisocial person?
produce.explain: Explain how knowing the prefix semi- can help you understand semicircle and semifinal. Give another word that uses semi-.

argue.prompt: Claim: Students should learn a few common prefixes instead of memorizing long word lists. Take a side and give two reasons using words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe students should / should not learn prefixes because ___. Knowing a prefix helps when ___.

constructed.prompt: Describe a day in a science class. Use antifreeze, supersonic, and transplant, and tell what each one does or means.
constructed.model: In science, we saw that antifreeze keeps a car's engine from freezing. We read about a supersonic jet that flies faster than the speed of sound. Then we learned to transplant seedlings from cups into the garden.

constructed.prompt: Describe a sports event at school. Use semifinal, postseason, and supervise, and explain who does what.
look: explains each in the sports setting
constructed.model: Our team played in the semifinal, one game before the championship. The postseason began after the regular games ended. The coach would supervise practice, watching to keep every player safe.

teacher.overview: Students learn five prefixes through ten words used across school subjects: anti- (against), post- (after), semi- (half), super- (above, beyond), and trans- (across). Each word has a clear prefix and a recognizable base, so students practice the method of breaking apart a word and predicting its meaning. The passage is a day of prefix hunting that moves through history, math, science, and sports.

notes.va.antisocial.adj: Anti- means against, so antisocial literally means against social contact. In everyday use, it means unfriendly or avoiding company; formally, it can also mean acting in ways that harm others. Be sure students do not label shy classmates this way. Teach that being quiet is not the same as being antisocial.
notes.va.antifreeze.n: Antifreeze keeps liquid in an engine from freezing. Connect anti- to against. Have students predict other anti- words, such as antiviral or antibiotic, and check them in a dictionary.
notes.va.postseason.n: Postseason is the set of games after the regular season. Post- means after. Contrast with preseason (before). Students may think the postseason is the off-season; clarify that it is the playoffs.
notes.va.postwar.adj: Postwar is an adjective that describes the time after a war. Post- means after. Ask students to name a postwar topic in history, such as new housing or changing jobs.
notes.va.semicircle.n: Semi- means half, so a semicircle is half of a circle. Draw a circle and cut it. Link to semicolon and semitruck to see the same prefix; point out that semicolon is half a colon in shape only, so the pattern is looser there.
notes.va.semifinal.n: A semifinal is the round or game before the final. Semi- here means half in the sense of half-way to the finish. Students may think a semifinal is a small game; clarify its place in the schedule.
notes.va.supersonic.adj: Supersonic means faster than the speed of sound. Super- means above or beyond. Sonic relates to sound. Link to the sound words from unit 3 and to ultrasonic. Ask what happens when a plane goes faster than sound.
notes.va.supervise.v: Supervise means to watch over and direct. Super- means over and vis relates to seeing, so a supervisor oversees. Students may confuse it with a superhero, so focus on the over idea.
notes.va.transplant.v: Transplant has a gardening sense, moving a plant, and a medical sense, moving an organ. Both use trans- (across). Keep the gardening sense first, then introduce the medical one so students are not surprised by it later.
notes.va.transfer.v: Transfer means to move across from one place or group to another. Students know a school transfer. Connect trans- to across and fer to carry. Ask students to name other things that can be transferred, such as money or a file.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The word is semifinal. I see semi- and final. Semi- means half, and final is the last. So a semifinal is a game that is partway to the last one. The text says it is the game before the championship, so I can check my guess against the clue.'
discuss: Which prefix on the list was already familiar to you from another word?
How does a prefix change a base word differently from a suffix?
misconceptions: Prefixes only change the beginning of a word and never its meaning.
Semi- always means half in a measured way.
Trans- only describes movement of people.
extend: Create a prefix poster with each of the five prefixes and a drawing for each word.
Invent a new word using one of the prefixes and write a definition and a sentence for it.
Hunt for prefix words in other classes for one week and add them to a class chart.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit telescope, microphone, aquatic, and thermal by asking students whether tele-, micro-, aqua, and therm are prefixes or roots, and how they differ from anti-, post-, semi-, super-, and trans-. Return to the five prefixes after two days, again at one week, with a word-hunt in a textbook.

wida.oral: Partner A says a base word, such as circle or season. Partner B adds one of the five prefixes, says the new word, and tells what it means.

needsReview: Prefix meanings (anti- against, post- after, semi- half, super- above or beyond, trans- across) are standard and well attested; the claim that supervise joins super- and a root vis meaning see is standard but was not checked against an etymological dictionary, and the spelling note (vis -> vise) is a simplification.

Antisocial: the unit teaches the everyday sense (unfriendly, not wanting company). The formal sense, acting against society, is mentioned in the teacher note. A human reviewer should confirm this framing is appropriate.
Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: postemporada (postseason), de posguerra (postwar), anticongelante (antifreeze), supervisar, trasplantar, transferir.
The semicolon note says it is half a colon in shape only; this is an informal teaching aid, not an etymological claim.
